## Setup

Do this before the workshop, on a network you trust. It takes about 10 minutes. After it, the workshop runs offline.

> **First, update Chrome to the latest version.** Open `chrome://settings/help`, let it download the update, and press **Relaunch**. WebMCP is an origin trial, and it changes from one Chrome release to the next. The workshop needs Chrome 155 or later and was checked in Chrome 157. Update even if you think you're current: Chrome often waits for a relaunch before it installs an update.

### You need

- **The latest Chrome: 155 or later.** Update at `chrome://settings/help`, then relaunch. Check the number at `chrome://version`. Chrome Beta or Canary work too.
- **Node 20.19 or later.** Check with `node --version`. Install the LTS from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org), or with `nvm install 22`.
- **git**, to clone the repo.
- **Port 5173 free.** The shop runs there.
- **A code editor.**
- **An AI coding agent, optional.** Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Antigravity or any other. The exercises work with or without one.

No accounts and no API keys. Nothing in the workshop calls a model: you call the tools yourself, from DevTools or from the workshop drawer in the page.

### Turn WebMCP on in Chrome

WebMCP is behind a flag. On `localhost`, the flag is all you need.

1. Open `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing` and set it to **Enabled**.
2. Open `chrome://flags/#devtools-webmcp-support`. If the flag is listed, set it to **Enabled** too. It adds the WebMCP pane to DevTools. If it isn't listed, your Chrome has the pane already.
3. Press **Relaunch**.

Check it: open DevTools on any page, and in the Console run:

```js
'modelContext' in document
```

It should print `true`.

### Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/apurvkhare/webmcp-workshop.git
cd webmcp-workshop
npm install
npm run doctor
```

`doctor` checks your Node version, the dependencies, the port, your Chrome version, and runs the finished app's tests. Every line should show ✓. Each ✗ says what to do. It can't see your Chrome flags: the next step checks those.

npm may print audit and deprecation warnings. They come from dev tools, and `doctor` passing means you can ignore them.

### Try it once

```bash
npm start -- --app app
```

Open <http://localhost:5173>. You should see Namma Bazaar, an online shop.

1. The **workshop drawer** is on the right of the page. If it is closed, the **Workshop** button at the right edge opens it. Next to its title is a green badge: **5 tools**.
2. Open the **Tools** tab. It lists the five tools.
3. Open `search_products`, and run it with `{ "query": "headphones" }`. Products come back as JSON, and the shop moves to the search results.
4. Open DevTools > **Application** > **WebMCP**. The same five tools are listed there.

Press `Ctrl+C` in the terminal to stop.

### If something is wrong

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| The drawer's badge says **WebMCP off** | The flag isn't on, or Chrome is older than 155. Do "Turn WebMCP on in Chrome" again, and use the **Relaunch** button: closing one window isn't enough |
| `'modelContext' in document` is `false`, but `'modelContext' in navigator` is `true` | Chrome is older than 152, where the API lived on `navigator`. Update Chrome |
| Running a tool fails with a `TypeError` about its input | Chrome is older than 155, where `executeTool` took a JSON string. Update Chrome |
| No **WebMCP** entry in DevTools > Application | Enable `chrome://flags/#devtools-webmcp-support` and relaunch. Or skip it: the drawer's Tools tab shows the same list and runs the same calls |
| The flags page is blocked, or Chrome is managed by your employer | Install Chrome Beta or Canary next to it. Or use a Chrome for Testing: see below |
| `npm start` says port 5173 is in use | Stop the other process, or run `npm start -- --port 5174` and use that port in every URL |
| `npm start` or `npm test` fails right after cloning | Run `npm run doctor` and follow its ✗ lines |
| The page is blank | Look at the terminal where `npm start` runs, and at the Console in DevTools. A syntax error in `playground/` shows in both |
| A tool you just wrote isn't in the list | Save the file and wait for the page to reload. Then check the Console: `registerTool` rejects a duplicate name, a name with spaces, and an empty description |
| The shop's data is in a strange state | Press **Reset demo data** in the drawer. It signs you out, empties the cart and forgets the orders |

#### A Chrome for Testing, if you can't change flags

This downloads a separate Chrome into the repo, and starts it with WebMCP on from the command line. It doesn't touch your own Chrome.

```bash
npx @puppeteer/browsers install chrome@stable --path .chrome
```

The command prints the path of the binary it installed. Start that binary with:

```
--enable-features=WebMCP,DevToolsWebMCPSupport
```

On macOS, for example:

```bash
"$(find .chrome -name 'Google Chrome for Testing' -type f | head -1)" --enable-features=WebMCP,DevToolsWebMCPSupport http://localhost:5173
```

### Not needed on localhost: the origin trial

A flag only changes your own browser. To give WebMCP to real users on a deployed site, you register for Chrome's **WebMCP origin trial** and put its token in the page. That is in [GOING-FURTHER.md](GOING-FURTHER.md). Nothing in the workshop needs it.

### If you'll use an agent

Open the repo in it once before the day, so it picks up `AGENTS.md`. That file keeps the agent to one step at a time, and has it explain its code. Try `/step 2.1` (Claude Code) or "do step 2.1" in any other agent, then reset with `npm run go 2.1`.

### Before you leave home

- [ ] Chrome is updated: `chrome://settings/help` says **Chrome is up to date**, and `chrome://version` says 155 or later
- [ ] `'modelContext' in document` prints `true`
- [ ] `npm run doctor` passes
- [ ] The drawer at localhost:5173 has a green **5 tools** badge
- [ ] Laptop charger

## How the workshop works

Each step is a pair of folders in `exercises/`: a **problem** with gaps marked 🔨, and its **solution**. You work in `playground/`.

```bash
npm run go 2.1      # load step 2.1 into playground/
npm start           # run the shop on http://localhost:5173
npm run status      # where you are, what's left, and whether the tests pass
npm test            # check the step
npm run go next     # on to the next step
```

Each step's `README.md` (also copied into `playground/`) has the task, how it works, what to look for, what breaks without it, and "Explain it back" questions.

The shop has a **workshop drawer** on the right of the page. If it is closed, the Workshop button at the right edge opens it. It is not part of the shop, and agents don't see it.

| Tab | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Guide | The current step's README. It switches by itself when you run `npm run go` |
| Tools | The tools the page has registered right now, with their schemas, and a form to run each one. The same as DevTools > Application > WebMCP |
| Activity | Every tool call the page logged (from step 6.1) |
| Agent view | What an agent has to read on this page, next to the tool list, and the two replays from section 1 |

Stuck? Read the 💡 hints in the code, then `npm run diff` to compare with the solution, then `npm run solution` to copy it in. Your own version is backed up to `.playground-backups/` first.

### The markers

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 🔨 | Build: what to write, with its step number (`🔨 4.2`) |
| 💡 | Hint: the shape of the answer |
| 🧠 | Why: the reason it works this way |
| 📡 | Look: what to find in DevTools > Application > WebMCP, or the drawer |
| 📖 | Docs: a spec or documentation link |
| 🧪 | Test: what `npm test` checks |
| 🔥 | Bonus: extra credit for fast finishers |
| ✅ | Done: work from an earlier step |

## 1 An agent goes shopping

No code in this section. Before you write any WebMCP, see how an agent does a shopping task today: by reading the page and clicking it. You give your own agent the task, and you ask it to tell you every step it took.

The task:

> Find wireless headphones under ₹5,000 rated 4 or higher, add the best-rated one that comes in black to the cart, apply the coupon DEVFEST10, and order it to my saved address in the earliest delivery slot.

### Run it

```bash
npm run go 2.1
```

```bash
npm start
```

If you did the setup check in the room, this is already running. Step 2.1's starting code registers no tools, so this is the shop as it is today, without WebMCP: the drawer says **0 tools**. Open <http://localhost:5173/?drawer=off>. `?drawer=off` hides the workshop drawer, so the agent sees only the shop. `?drawer=on` brings it back.

### Give your agent the task

Use any agent that can drive a browser: Antigravity's browser agent, Claude Code or Codex with Chrome DevTools MCP or Claude in Chrome, or another. The setup for each is in [demo/README.md](demo/README.md#with-a-coding-agent-instead). Give it this:

```text
Open http://localhost:5173/?drawer=off in the browser and do this task on the page:

Find wireless headphones under ₹5,000 rated 4 or higher, add the best-rated one that comes in black to the cart, apply the coupon DEVFEST10, and order it to my saved address in the earliest delivery slot.

Use only the browser. Don't read this project's code and don't call the shop's API.

When you're done, list every step you took, numbered: each time you read the page, and each click, key press or text you typed. Say where you had to look for something, guess or try again. Then give the totals.
```

The answer, to check it against: Tarang Studio Pro Wireless Headphones in black, ₹4,319 after the coupon, order **NB-1001**. Before you try again, reset the shop: open <http://localhost:5173/?drawer=on> and press **Reset demo data** in the drawer, or run `curl -X POST http://localhost:5173/api/dev/reset`.

No agent with a browser? Do the task by hand and count your clicks, then watch the presenter's run. A recording of one, with its step list, is in [demo/recordings](demo/recordings/agent-without-webmcp.md).

### Read what it tells you

- **How did it see the page?** Screenshots read by a vision model, the HTML DOM, or the accessibility tree (roles, names and states). Most agents mix them. The recording used screenshots 14 times and the accessibility tree once, and never read the HTML.
- **How many steps, and how many of them were reading?** Every action is followed by a read, because the agent can't know what changed.
- **Where did it have to look?** The coupon box is collapsed. Checkout sends you to sign in first. The results show colour dots, not names.
- **What did it read that wasn't for it?** One review on the black headphones is written to AI assistants.
- **Who confirmed the order?** Nothing in the page knows an agent is there, so nothing stops it at Place order.

On the projector, the presenter runs an agent the same way, or plays the recording. Keep your agent's step list: in section 7 you run the same task again, with the tools you wrote.

### 🧠 What to take from it

- **An agent can already use your site.** It does it the way a person would, through the page, with no help from you.
- **It pays for that in reading.** Each step is a screenshot or a page read, and most of what it reads isn't what it needs.
- **It depends on the page.** Move a button, rename a label, add a banner, and it may break. With WebMCP the agent depends on a contract instead: a name, a description and a schema. That is what you write from section 2 on.
- **The page can't tell it from a person.** So it can't ask the shopper before the order goes out, or log what the agent did.

### Explain it back

1. How many steps did your agent take, and how many of them were reads?
2. Where did it have to search, guess or go back?
3. Which step should it not have done without asking you, and why couldn't the page stop it?

**Next:** step 2.1 is already in your playground. Read `playground/README.md`. `npm start` keeps running.

<!-- from exercises/02.register-tools/README.md -->

## 2 Register tools

A WebMCP tool is a JavaScript function your page hands to the browser, with a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its input. An agent in the browser sees the list and calls them. You write two.

| Step | You write | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | `search_products`: name, description, `inputSchema`, `execute`, then `registerTool()` | `webmcp/catalog-tools.ts` |
| 2.2 | `add_to_cart`: `required` in the schema, input checks, errors returned as text | `webmcp/cart-tools.ts` |

By the end, an agent can find a product and put it in the cart without reading a single page.

```
 agent ── getTools() ──────────────▶ browser ── the page's registered tools
 agent ── executeTool(tool, input) ─▶ browser ── execute(input) in your page ──▶ fetch('/api/…') with the shopper's cookie
```

The tool runs in the tab, as the shopper. It calls the same `shop` functions the buttons call, so there is no second backend and no new auth.

Start with `npm run go 2.1`, and keep `npm start` running in another terminal.

---

<!-- from exercises/02.register-tools/01.problem.search-products/README.md -->

## 2.1 Register search_products with a JSON Schema

🔨 **Your task:** Describe a `search_products` tool and register it with `document.modelContext.registerTool()`.

**Where:** `webmcp/catalog-tools.ts`: the 🔨 2.1 marker, inside `registerCatalogTools`.

### Where you start

Namma Bazaar is a working shop: search, product pages, a cart, checkout. Open it at <http://localhost:5173> and click around.

`webmcp/index.ts` has `setupWebMCP(shop)`, which the shop calls once when the page has loaded. It calls `registerCatalogTools(shop)`, and that function is empty. The page offers an agent nothing: the drawer's **Tools** tab says so.

`shop` is the page's own API, the one the buttons use: `shop.searchProducts(filters)` fetches from the server, and `shop.ui.showSearch(filters)` navigates the page to the results.

### 🧠 How it works

**A tool is a plain object.** Four fields matter:

```ts
const searchProducts: ModelContextTool = {
  name: 'search_products',
  description: '…',
  inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { … } },
  async execute(input) { … }
};
await document.modelContext.registerTool(searchProducts);
```

**`name`** is how the agent refers to the tool. Up to 128 characters: letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`. Chrome rejects anything else, and a name that is already registered.

**`description`** is the only documentation the agent gets. Say what the tool does, what comes back, and what to do with it next ("pass an id to add_to_cart"). Chrome rejects an empty one.

**`inputSchema`** is a JSON Schema for one object. Give every property a `type` and a `description`. `enum` lists the allowed values, which here are the shop's categories.

**`execute(input)`** runs in the page, in the shopper's tab, with their session. It calls `shop.searchProducts(input)`, which is an ordinary `fetch` with the shopper's cookie. Nothing new is exposed: the tool can do what the shopper can already do by clicking.

**Return a string.** That string is what the agent reads. Chrome turns an object into JSON text for you, and `undefined` into the word "undefined", so decide yourself. Keep it small: eight products with six fields each, not the whole catalogue.

**The page follows the agent.** `shop.ui.showSearch(input)` moves the page to the same results, so the shopper sees what the agent is looking at.

**`registerTool()` returns a promise.** It rejects if the name is invalid or already taken, or the description is empty.

### 📡 What to look for

Open DevTools > **Application** > **WebMCP**, or the drawer's **Tools** tab. `search_products` is listed with its description and schema.

Run it with:

```json
{ "query": "wireless headphones", "maxPrice": 5000, "minRating": 4 }
```

Four products come back as JSON, and the page behind the drawer moves to the search results.

In the console, this is what an agent does:

```js
const [tool] = await document.modelContext.getTools();
await document.modelContext.executeTool(tool, { query: 'keyboard' });
```

### What breaks without it

Without a tool, an agent has to read the page, find the search box, type, wait, and read the page again. You'll see that in section 1's replay. Without a schema, it has to guess what to send. Without a description, it doesn't know the tool is worth calling.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that the tool is registered, that its schema has the four properties with descriptions, and that a search answers with the matching products as JSON text.

### Explain it back

Answer these in your own words, or have your agent answer them, quoting the lines it wrote.

1. Where does `execute` run, and whose session does its `fetch` use?
2. What does the agent know about `search_products` before it calls it?
3. Why return eight short summaries instead of the full product records?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: registerTool](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [Chrome for Developers: WebMCP](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp)

<!-- from exercises/02.register-tools/02.problem.add-to-cart/README.md -->

## 2.2 Validate input in add_to_cart

🔨 **Your task:** Mark `productId` and `colour` as required in `add_to_cart`'s schema, check the input inside `execute`, and return every problem as a sentence the agent can act on.

**Where:** `webmcp/cart-tools.ts`: the two 🔨 2.2 markers, in `add_to_cart`.

### Where you start

There is a new file, `webmcp/cart-tools.ts`, with three tools: `view_cart`, `add_to_cart` and `apply_coupon`. `webmcp/index.ts` registers them.

`add_to_cart` passes whatever it is given straight to `shop.addToCart()`. Try it from the Tools tab with a colour the product doesn't come in:

```json
{ "productId": "hp-103", "colour": "black" }
```

The call fails, and all the agent is told is that the tool failed.

### 🧠 How it works

**Chrome does not check input against your schema.** The schema is documentation for the agent. If the agent sends `quantity: "two"`, or leaves out `colour`, `execute` gets exactly that. So the schema says what you expect, and `execute` checks that it got it.

**`required`** lists the properties that must be sent. A good agent follows it. A sloppy one doesn't, which is why you check anyway.

**Return the problem, don't throw it.** When `execute` throws, the agent gets a generic failure with none of your message: Chrome logs the real error to the page's console and tells the agent only that the invocation failed. A returned string reaches the agent as written. So return a sentence that starts with `Error:` and says how to fix the call:

```
Error: Dhwani Bass 500 Wireless Headphones comes in blue, red. Pass one of those as colour.
```

An agent that reads that can try again. An agent that reads "the invocation failed" can only give up, or guess.

**Check what the server would reject, and say it better.** Three checks cover most bad calls: the product exists, it comes in that colour, and the quantity is a whole number from 1 to 5.

**The server still decides.** Out of stock, or more than five of one product in the cart: the shop's API refuses those, and `shop.addToCart()` throws a `ShopError`. `errorText(error)` turns it into an `Error: …` sentence. Your checks make better messages. They don't replace the server's rules, because the agent isn't the only caller.

### 📡 What to look for

In the WebMCP pane or the Tools tab, run `add_to_cart` three times:

| Input | Answer |
|---|---|
| `{ "productId": "hp-103", "colour": "black" }` | An error that lists blue and red |
| `{ "productId": "hp-102", "colour": "black", "quantity": "two" }` | An error about the quantity |
| `{ "productId": "hp-102", "colour": "black" }` | "Added 1 × …", and the cart badge in the header goes up |

### What breaks without it

The agent sends a colour that doesn't exist, the call throws, and the agent learns nothing. It retries the same call, or tells the shopper the site is broken.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that `productId` and `colour` are required, that a good call adds to the cart, and that an unknown id, a wrong colour, a bad quantity and an out-of-stock product each return `Error: …` without throwing.

### Explain it back

1. What does Chrome do when an agent's input doesn't match `inputSchema`?
2. What does the agent receive when `execute` throws, and what does it receive when `execute` returns `Error: …`?
3. Which bad inputs do you catch in `execute`, and which does the server catch? Why both?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: executing a tool](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [JSON Schema: required](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/object#required)

## ✅ Section 2 done

The page now offers four tools: `search_products`, `view_cart`, `add_to_cart` and `apply_coupon`. An agent can find a product and put it in the cart with two calls.

### Talk it over

- `search_products` returns eight products. What should it do when forty match? Who should decide: the tool, or the agent?
- Chrome doesn't validate input against the schema. If it did, which of your checks could you delete, and which would you keep?
- Every tool calls the same `shop` functions the buttons call. What would go wrong if a tool talked to a different endpoint from the UI?

<!-- from exercises/03.form-tool/README.md -->

## 3 Turn a form into a tool

You already have forms. Each one is a list of named, typed, labelled inputs with a submit action, which is most of a tool definition. In Chrome, two attributes on the `<form>` make it one, with no `registerTool()` call.

| Step | You write | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | `toolname` and `tooldescription` on the form, `toolparamdescription` on two fields, and `respondWith()` in the submit handler | `ui/AddressForm.tsx` |

By the end, an agent can fill in the delivery address on the checkout page. The shopper still presses Save.

```
 agent ── executeTool(set_delivery_address, { … }) ─▶ Chrome fills the fields
                                                       shopper presses Save
 agent ◀── "Saved the delivery address: …" ────────── respondWith(result)
```

> **This part is Chrome-only, and it is no longer in the WebMCP specification.** The declarative API was taken out of the spec draft on 8 October 2026 while its design is reworked. Chrome still ships it behind the same flag and origin trial. It is here because it shows the idea well and works today. Don't build a product on it yet: the imperative API from section 2 is the stable part.

Start with `npm run go 3.1`.

---

<!-- from exercises/03.form-tool/01.problem.address-form/README.md -->

## 3.1 Make the address form a tool

🔨 **Your task:** Turn the delivery address form into a tool named `set_delivery_address`: name and describe the form, describe two of its fields, and give the agent an answer when it submits.

**Where:** `ui/AddressForm.tsx`: four 🔨 3.1 markers. Two on the `<form>` and its submit handler, two on the phone and PIN code inputs.

### Where you start

Sign in (the **Sign in** link, then one click: the demo shopper has no password), add something to the cart, and go to checkout. The first step is the address form in `ui/AddressForm.tsx`: six fields, a **Save and continue** button, and an `onSubmit` that calls `save(form)`.

`save()` already returns a promise for one sentence: `Saved the delivery address: …`, or `Error: …` when the server refuses the address. Nothing uses that sentence yet.

An agent has no tool for the address. Check the Tools tab while you are on the checkout page.

### 🧠 How it works

**`toolname` and `tooldescription` on a `<form>` register it as a tool.** Chrome does the registering. The tool exists while the form is in the page and goes away when the form does, so `set_delivery_address` is only offered on the checkout page.

**Chrome builds the input schema from the fields.** Each field's `name` becomes a property. `required` puts it in the schema's `required` list. A `<select>` becomes an `enum` of its option values. The property's `description` is the field's `<label>` text.

**`toolparamdescription` replaces the label as the description.** "Mobile number" is enough for a person, who can see the placeholder and the error message. An agent needs the format: ten digits, no country code.

**The agent fills, the shopper submits.** When an agent calls the tool, Chrome puts the values in the fields, focuses the submit button and waits. The call finishes only when the shopper presses Save. That is the confirmation step, and you get it for free. `toolautosubmit` on the form removes it: Chrome submits by itself. Use that only for forms where a wrong submit costs nothing, such as a search box.

**The agent needs an answer.** A form submit normally ends in a navigation, and Chrome gives the agent the page that results. This shop is a single-page app: `onSubmit` calls `preventDefault()` and saves with `fetch`. So you tell Chrome what the answer is:

```ts
const submit = event.nativeEvent as SubmitEvent;
if (submit.agentInvoked) submit.respondWith(result);
```

`agentInvoked` is `true` when an agent filled the form. `respondWith()` takes a promise for the tool's result. It only works after `preventDefault()`.

**`event.nativeEvent`** is the browser's own `SubmitEvent`. React wraps events, and the wrapper doesn't have these two members.

**In React, the attributes are written as they are in HTML**, all lowercase: `toolname`, not `toolName`. `shop/src/react-webmcp.d.ts` adds them to the JSX types so TypeScript accepts them.

### 📡 What to look for

On the checkout page, open DevTools > Application > WebMCP, or the Tools tab. `set_delivery_address` is listed. Look at its schema: you didn't write it. Find `phone`'s description, the `enum` for `addressType`, and the `required` list.

Run it:

```json
{ "fullName": "Apurv Khare", "phone": "9845011111", "line1": "221, 12th Main, Koramangala", "city": "Bengaluru", "pincode": "560034", "addressType": "work" }
```

The fields fill in and the form is outlined: the shop's CSS styles `form:tool-form-active`. The Save button is focused and highlighted, and the call is still running. Press **Save and continue**, and the answer arrives: "Saved the delivery address: …".

Run it again with `"line1": "221"`. The browser's form validation accepts that, and the shop's server doesn't. After you press the button, the agent gets `Error: The address isn't complete: …`.

### What breaks without it

Without `toolname`, the agent has to find six inputs on the page and type into each one. Without `respondWith()`, the address is saved but the agent is never told, and its call ends without a result.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks the attributes on the form and the two fields, that an agent's submit is answered with the "Saved the delivery address…" sentence, that a refused address is answered with `Error: …`, and that a person's submit never calls `respondWith()`.

The tests can't check what Chrome does with the attributes. `npm run verify:chrome -- --only 3.1` does that against the solution, in a real Chrome.

### Explain it back

1. Where does `set_delivery_address`'s input schema come from? Name three things in the form that end up in it.
2. Who submits the form when an agent calls the tool, and what would `toolautosubmit` change?
3. Why does this form need `respondWith()`, when a form that navigates to a new page doesn't?

### 📖 Read more

- [Chrome for Developers: WebMCP declarative API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp)
- [The spec change that removed it, for now](https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp/pull/338)

<!-- from exercises/04.user-control/README.md -->

## 4 Keep the user in control

An agent acts for the shopper, in the shopper's session. The page decides how much it can do unasked. You tell agents what each tool does, and you put a question in front of the shopper before the one call that spends their money.

| Step | You write | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | `readOnlyHint` on the tools that only read, `untrustedContentHint` on `get_reviews` | `webmcp/catalog-tools.ts`, `webmcp/cart-tools.ts` |
| 4.2 | `consequentialHint` on `place_order`, and a confirmation dialog inside `execute` | `webmcp/order-tools.ts` |

Four things to know before you start:

- **Annotations are hints.** They tell an agent, and the browser, what kind of tool this is. They stop nothing.
- **Chrome shows no prompt of its own.** `consequentialHint` doesn't make Chrome ask the user anything today.
- **`requestUserInteraction()` is gone.** Older posts show it. It was removed from the spec and from Chrome. A confirmation is something you build in your page.
- **Tool results can carry text from strangers.** A review, a message, a username. An agent that reads it may take it for instructions.

Start with `npm run go 4.1`.

---

<!-- from exercises/04.user-control/01.problem.annotations/README.md -->

## 4.1 Say what each tool does with annotations

🔨 **Your task:** Mark the tools that only read with `readOnlyHint`, and mark `get_reviews` with `untrustedContentHint` as well.

**Where:** `webmcp/catalog-tools.ts`: two 🔨 4.1 markers, on `search_products` and `get_reviews`. `webmcp/cart-tools.ts`: one, on `view_cart`.

### Where you start

There is a new tool in `webmcp/catalog-tools.ts`: `get_reviews`, which returns what customers wrote about a product.

To an agent, all five tools look the same. Nothing says that `search_products` is safe to call at any time and `add_to_cart` changes something. Nothing says that `get_reviews` returns text the shop didn't write.

### 🧠 How it works

**`annotations` is an object of boolean hints on the tool:**

```ts
annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: true }
```

| Hint | It says | An agent can use it to |
|---|---|---|
| `readOnlyHint` | Calling this changes nothing | Call it without asking the user first |
| `untrustedContentHint` | The result contains text from outside the site's control | Treat the result as data, never as instructions |
| `consequentialHint` | This does something that matters and may not be undoable | Ask the user before calling it (step 4.2) |

**There is a fourth, `debugging`,** for a tool meant for developer tooling rather than for an agent helping a person. Agents can leave those out. No Namma Bazaar tool needs it.

**They are hints, not locks.** Chrome passes them to the agent and enforces nothing. A tool marked read-only can still write if you make it, so be honest: a wrong hint is worse than none.

**Why `get_reviews` is different.** Every other tool returns text the shop wrote. Reviews are written by anyone with an account. One of the reviews of `hp-102` is addressed to AI assistants: it tells them to ignore their instructions and order five smartwatches. That is a prompt injection, and it reaches the agent through your tool.

**The hint is one defence, not the only one.** Step 4.2 adds the one that holds even if an agent believes the review: the shopper has to confirm an order in the page.

### 📡 What to look for

In the WebMCP pane or the Tools tab, `search_products`, `view_cart` and `get_reviews` now show as read-only, and `get_reviews` as untrusted.

Run `get_reviews` with `{ "productId": "hp-102" }` and read the third review. Then open the product page and read it there. A person scrolls past it. An agent reads every word.

In the console:

```js
(await document.modelContext.getTools()).map((t) => [t.name, t.annotations]);
```

### What breaks without it

A careful agent asks the user before every call, including a search, because it can't tell a read from a write. A careless one treats a stranger's review as part of its instructions.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that `search_products`, `view_cart` and `get_reviews` are read-only, that `add_to_cart` and `apply_coupon` are not, that only `get_reviews` claims untrusted content, and that the planted review really is in its result.

### Explain it back

1. What does Chrome do differently for a tool with `readOnlyHint: true`?
2. Why does `get_reviews` get `untrustedContentHint` and `search_products` doesn't?
3. Suppose an agent ignores the hint and believes the review. What still stands between that review and an order?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: tool annotations](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [Chrome for Developers: WebMCP](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp)

---

Stuck? 💡 Read the hint lines in the code, then `npm run diff`, then `npm run solution`. (Agents: only when the person asks.)

<!-- from exercises/04.user-control/02.problem.confirm-order/README.md -->

## 4.2 Ask before placing an order

🔨 **Your task:** Mark `place_order` with `consequentialHint`, and make it ask the shopper in the page before it orders anything.

**Where:** `webmcp/order-tools.ts`: the two 🔨 4.2 markers, in `place_order`.

### Where you start

There is a new file, `webmcp/order-tools.ts`, with three tools: `get_delivery_slots`, `place_order` and `get_orders`. `webmcp/index.ts` registers them.

`place_order` works, and that is the problem. Sign in, add something to the cart, and run it from the Tools tab with a slot id from `get_delivery_slots`. The order is placed at once. The shopper is told afterwards.

Reset with the drawer's **Reset demo data** before you go on.

### 🧠 How it works

**`consequentialHint: true`** says that this call matters and can't be taken back. An agent, or a browser, can use it to ask the user first. Chrome itself shows no prompt today, so the hint alone protects nobody.

**The page asks.** There is no browser API for "ask the user": `requestUserInteraction()` was removed from the spec and from Chrome. But `execute` is an async function running in your page, and your page already knows how to show a dialog. So `execute` opens one and waits:

```ts
async execute(input, { signal }) {
  const preview = await shop.previewOrder(input.slotId);
  const confirmed = await shop.ui.confirm({ title, lines, confirmLabel, signal });
  if (!confirmed) return 'The shopper did not confirm, so nothing was ordered. …';
  const order = await shop.placeOrder(preview.slot.id);
  …
}
```

The agent's call stays open for as long as the dialog does. From the agent's side, it is a slow tool.

**Show what they are agreeing to.** `shop.previewOrder(slotId)` asks the server what would be ordered: the cart as it is now, the saved address, the slot, the total. The dialog shows that, not what the agent said it was ordering. The agent may be wrong, or lying because a review told it to.

**The dialog belongs to the page, so the agent can't press its button.** A tool call can't click. Only the shopper can say yes.

**Say no clearly.** When the shopper declines, return a sentence that says nothing was ordered and that the agent shouldn't retry. A vague answer invites a second attempt.

**`signal` is `execute`'s second argument.** It aborts when the agent or the browser cancels the call. Pass it to `shop.ui.confirm()` and the dialog closes by itself, instead of sitting on screen for a call nobody is waiting for.

**The server is still the authority.** `shop.placeOrder()` is refused by the server if nobody is signed in, the cart is empty, or there is no address. The dialog is for the shopper's consent. It isn't the security boundary.

### 📡 What to look for

Sign in, add something to the cart, and run `get_delivery_slots`, then `place_order` with the first slot's id.

1. A dialog opens over the page with the items, the address, the slot and the total. The tool call is still running.
2. Press **Not now**. The agent's answer says nothing was ordered. The Orders page is empty.
3. Run it again and confirm. The answer has an order number, and the page shows the order.

### What breaks without it

An agent that misread the request, or believed the review from step 4.1, places an order the shopper never saw. On this shop it is cash on delivery. On yours it may be a card.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that `place_order` is marked consequential, that declining orders nothing, that the dialog shows the items and the total, that confirming places the order, that cancelling the call closes the dialog, and that an empty cart is refused without asking.

### Explain it back

1. What does Chrome do when an agent calls a tool that has `consequentialHint: true`?
2. Why does the dialog show `preview`, which comes from the server, rather than the agent's input?
3. What happens to the dialog, and to the order, if the agent cancels the call while the dialog is open?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: tool annotations and execute](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [MDN: AbortSignal](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal)

---

Stuck? 💡 Read the hint lines in the code, then `npm run diff`, then `npm run solution`. (Agents: only when the person asks.)

- `add_to_cart` has no confirmation. Should it? Where is the line on a site you work on?

<!-- from exercises/05.tool-lifecycle/README.md -->

## 5 Tools follow state

The list of tools is not fixed. It is a description of what can be done on this page, right now, by this user. When that changes, the list should change with it.

| Step | You write | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | The order tools registered at sign-in with an `AbortSignal`, and removed by aborting it at sign-out | `webmcp/index.ts`, `webmcp/order-tools.ts` |

There is no `unregisterTool()`. A tool is registered with a signal, and it lives until that signal aborts:

```
 sign in  ──▶ controller = new AbortController()
              registerTool(tool, { signal: controller.signal })   × 3
 sign out ──▶ controller.abort()                                  all three are gone
```

Start with `npm run go 5.1`.

---

<!-- from exercises/05.tool-lifecycle/01.problem.signed-in-tools/README.md -->

## 5.1 Register order tools only while signed in

🔨 **Your task:** Register `get_delivery_slots`, `place_order` and `get_orders` when someone signs in, and unregister them when they sign out.

**Where:** `webmcp/order-tools.ts`: one 🔨 5.1 marker, on `registerOrderTools`. `webmcp/index.ts`: one, at the end of `setupWebMCP`.

### Where you start

`setupWebMCP` registers every tool when the page loads, signed in or not.

Sign out and look at the Tools tab: `place_order` is still offered. Run it, and the answer is `Error: Nobody is signed in. The shopper has to sign in first.` The server refused, which is right. But the agent was offered something it can't do, spent a call finding that out, and now has to explain it to the shopper.

### 🧠 How it works

**`registerTool` takes a second argument:**

```ts
document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal });
```

`signal` is an `AbortSignal`. When it aborts, the tool is unregistered. That is the only way to remove a tool: there is no `unregisterTool()`.

**One controller for a group of tools.** Register all three order tools with the same signal, and one `abort()` removes all three. You don't keep a list.

**A controller is used once.** After `abort()`, its signal stays aborted. For the next sign-in you make a new `AbortController`.

**`shop.getUser()` and `shop.onUserChange(listener)`.** The first is who is signed in right now, or `null`. The second calls your listener at every sign-in and sign-out. You need both: the page may load with the shopper already signed in, so check once at the start, then listen.

**Don't register twice.** A second `registerTool` with a name that is already registered is rejected with `InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name`. Keep the controller in a variable. If it is set, the tools are registered.

**The browser tells agents.** Each registration and each removal fires `toolchange` on `document.modelContext`, so an agent's list stays current without a reload.

**This is for the agent's benefit, not for security.** The server refuses an order from a signed-out session whether or not the tool is listed. Removing the tool keeps the list honest: it shows what can be done now.

The same pattern fits anything that comes and goes: tools for an open editor, for a page of a single-page app, for a role.

### 📡 What to look for

Keep DevTools > Application > WebMCP open, or the Tools tab.

1. Signed out: five tools. No `get_delivery_slots`, `get_orders` or `place_order`.
2. Sign in: eight tools, with no reload.
3. Sign out: back to five.
4. Sign in again: eight, and no error in the console.

In the console, before you sign in:

```js
document.modelContext.addEventListener('toolchange', async () =>
  console.log((await document.modelContext.getTools()).map((t) => t.name)));
```

### What breaks without it

Signed out, an agent is offered `place_order`, calls it, and gets an error. Worse, on a site where tools depend on the page: a tool for an editor that is no longer open runs against nothing.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that the three tools are absent while signed out, present after sign-in, gone after sign-out, back after the next sign-in with each registered once, present straight away when the page loads signed in, and that `toolchange` fires.

### Explain it back

1. How do you unregister a tool? What is there instead of `unregisterTool()`?
2. Why does `sync` run once straight away, as well as on every change?
3. What would happen at the second sign-in if you reused the first `AbortController`?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: registerTool options](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [MDN: AbortController](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)

---

Stuck? 💡 Read the hint lines in the code, then `npm run diff`, then `npm run solution`. (Agents: only when the person asks.)

<!-- from exercises/06.observability/README.md -->

## 6 See what agents do

Your server sees API requests. It can't tell whether a person clicked or an agent called a tool: both are the same `fetch` with the same cookie. The page is the only place that knows. So the page logs.

| Step | You write | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | `withLogging(tool, log)`: a wrapper that records each call's tool, input, duration and outcome | `webmcp/logging.ts` |

By the end, every tool call shows up in the drawer's **Activity** tab and in the terminal where `npm start` runs.

```
 agent ── executeTool ─▶ withLogging(tool).execute ─▶ tool.execute ─▶ result
                                   │
                                   └─▶ shop.log.record({ tool, input, outcome, ms })
                                          ├─▶ the Activity tab
                                          └─▶ POST /api/agent-log ─▶ the terminal
```

Start with `npm run go 6.1`.

---

<!-- from exercises/06.observability/01.problem.log-calls/README.md -->

## 6.1 Log every tool call

🔨 **Your task:** Write `withLogging(tool, log)`: it returns a copy of a tool whose `execute` records what happened and passes the result on unchanged.

**Where:** `webmcp/logging.ts`: the 🔨 6.1 marker.

### Where you start

There is a new file, `webmcp/logging.ts`, and every `registerTool` call in the three tool files now reads `registerTool(withLogging(tool, shop.log))`. For now `withLogging` returns the tool as it is, so nothing is logged.

Run a few tools and open the drawer's **Activity** tab: it is empty. So is the terminal.

`shop.log.record(entry)` is ready to use. It adds a line to the Activity tab and posts it to the shop's server, which prints it.

### 🧠 How it works

**A tool is a plain object, so you can wrap it.** Copy everything, replace `execute`:

```ts
return {
  ...tool,
  async execute(input, options) {
    const result = await tool.execute(input, options);
    …
    return result;
  }
};
```

The name, description, schema and annotations stay as they were. The agent can't tell the difference.

**What to record.** The tool's name, the input, how long it took, and how it ended:

| `outcome` | When |
|---|---|
| `'ok'` | `execute` returned |
| `'error'` | `execute` returned text that starts with `Error:` (your convention from step 2.2) |
| `'threw'` | `execute` threw. Record it, then throw the same error again |

**Logging must not change what the agent gets.** Return exactly what the tool returned. Rethrow exactly what it threw. Pass `options` through, or `place_order` loses the `signal` that closes its dialog.

**Why in the page.** The server sees `POST /api/cart/items`. It can't tell an agent's call from a click. It also never sees a call that failed your checks in `execute` and returned an error before any request was made. Only the page sees every call, with the input the agent actually sent.

**What the log is for.** Which tools agents use, and which they never find. Which calls fail, and with what input, which tells you where a description or a schema is unclear. How long the shopper took to confirm an order.

**Inputs can hold personal data.** A product id is harmless. An address, a message or a search for a medicine isn't. Here everything is logged, because it is a workshop. In production, choose the fields.

**The form tool has no `execute` to wrap.** Chrome registers `set_delivery_address` from the form, so it never passes through `withLogging`. The 🔥 bonus in `webmcp/index.ts` covers it: the browser fires `toolactivated` on `document.modelContext` for every tool call, and `toolcancel` when one is cancelled.

### 📡 What to look for

Run `search_products`, then `add_to_cart` with a colour the product doesn't come in, then `add_to_cart` correctly.

- The drawer's **Activity** tab has three lines, newest first: the tool, the outcome, the milliseconds, and the input and result when you open one.
- The terminal where `npm start` runs has the same three lines, each starting with 🤖.

Then sign in and run `place_order`. Wait a few seconds before you confirm. The `ms` is the time the shopper took.

### What breaks without it

Agents use your site and you can't see it. A tool whose description confuses every agent fails all day, and nothing in your server logs looks unusual.

### 🧪 Check it

`npm test` checks that each call logs one line with the tool, input, outcome, `ms` and result, that an `Error:` answer is logged as `'error'`, that the agent gets exactly what the tool returned, that a throw is logged as `'threw'` and still throws, and that the rest of the tool is unchanged.

### Explain it back

1. Why can't the server tell an agent's request from a person's?
2. What are the three outcomes, and how does the wrapper tell `'ok'` from `'error'`?
3. What would go wrong for `place_order` if the wrapper didn't pass `options` on?

### 📖 Read more

- [WebMCP specification: toolactivated and toolcancel events](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/)
- [MDN: performance.now()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/now)

## 7 Replay and ship

No code in this section. You run the opening task again, this time with the tools you wrote, and then look at what it takes to put this on a real site.

### Replay it

Your playground should be on step 6.1 with every test passing:

```bash
npm run status
```

With `npm start` running, open the drawer's **Agent view** tab and press **Shop with tools**. Confirm the order when the dialog asks.

Each line of the run is a step you wrote:

| The run does | You wrote it in |
|---|---|
| `search_products` with a query, a price and a rating | 2.1 |
| `add_to_cart` with the id and the colour | 2.2 |
| `apply_coupon` | given |
| `get_delivery_slots`, only there because the script signed in first | 5.1 |
| `place_order`, which waits for you | 4.2 |
| A line for each call in the Activity tab and the terminal | 6.1 |

If the run stops early, it says which tool it couldn't find. `npm run status` tells you which step that is.

### Compare it with section 1

In section 1 your agent did this task by reading and clicking the page. Now put the two side by side:

1. **Look at the top of the Agent view tab.** It shows what an agent has to read on this page: the page as text, next to the list of tools. Both have a size. Go to another page and watch the first number change and the second stay put.
2. **Press Shop by clicking.** A script does the task through the UI, the way your agent did. Each step is highlighted as it happens.
3. **Press Shop with tools** again, and read the table. It has the steps and the amount of text read for each run.
4. **Hold it against your agent's step list from section 1.** The replay is a script, not a model, so its numbers are not a benchmark. A real agent takes more steps both ways.

On the projector, the presenter gives the same task to Gemini in the Model Context Tool Inspector, on the finished shop. Gemini gets the tool list, not the page, and makes five or six calls. The runbook is in [demo/README.md](demo/README.md#run-2-in-section-7-gemini-with-the-shops-tools). Anyone with a Gemini key can do the same: install the Inspector, run `npm start -- --app app --port 5174`, and give it the task.

Both runs end with the same order. WebMCP doesn't make something possible that wasn't. It changes how much the agent reads, how many steps it takes, how much can go wrong on the way, and who confirms the order.

### Try to break it

- In the Tools tab, run `place_order` and press **Not now**. Read what the agent is told.
- Sign out and look at the tool list.
- Run `get_reviews` for `hp-102` and find the review that isn't for you.
- Turn the flag off at `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing`, relaunch, and use the shop. Nothing is broken: `setupWebMCP` returns early, and the page is an ordinary shop. Turn the flag back on.

### Ship it

The [production checklist](PRODUCTION-CHECKLIST.md) is the handout. The short version:

- **Feature-detect.** `if (!('modelContext' in document)) return;` The site must work without WebMCP: most browsers don't have it.
- **A tool is a way into code the user can already run.** It adds no permission. The server authorises every request as before.
- **Validate in `execute`.** Chrome doesn't. Return errors as text the agent can act on.
- **Ask in the page before anything that costs money or can't be undone.** Annotations are hints.
- **Keep the tool list true.** Register with a signal, abort it when the state changes.
- **Log calls in the page.** Nothing else can tell an agent from a person.
- **It is an origin trial.** In Chrome until at least Chrome 162, and in Edge from Edge 150, behind a flag or a token. ChatGPT Desktop and Brave's Leo AI call WebMCP tools too. The API has changed shape before and may again. Read the spec before each release.

### Where to go next

[GOING-FURTHER.md](GOING-FURTHER.md) has what didn't fit: a real model calling your tools from the Model Context Tool Inspector, automated agent tests with Chrome DevTools MCP, tools in cross-origin iframes, the W3C polyfill for other browsers, and deploying with an origin trial token.

### Explain it back

1. Which of your tools would you ship as they are, and which would you change first?
2. What does a user of Firefox or Safari see on a site that has WebMCP tools?
3. What would you check in the spec before your next release, and why?
